summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing devices that run the Internet Group Management Protocol for IPv4 and Multicast Listener Discovery for IPv6. These protocols are used by hosts and routers to manage multicast group membership.

eli5.summary: IGMP and MLD are how computers tell the network which group broadcasts they want. This gives a standard form to set up and check those settings on a device.

how to configure igmp with netconf
what is mld in ipv6 multicast
subtitle: A standard YANG model for configuring and monitoring IGMP and MLD, the protocols hosts use to join multicast groups.

tldr.problem: Routers that run IGMP for IPv4 and MLD for IPv6 each had their own vendor-specific way to be configured and monitored.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module, ietf-igmp-mld, augments the core routing model with separate igmp and mld containers holding configuration, operational state, statistics and a clear-groups action, with less common features marked optional.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get one common data model for IGMPv1 to v3 and MLDv1 and v2 over NETCONF or RESTCONF. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8652 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2019. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
YANG is a data definition language for devices managed with protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. This RFC defines a YANG data model to configure and manage IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) and MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery) devices. It covers IGMPv1, IGMPv2, IGMPv3, MLDv1 and MLDv2. Core features are required and non-core features are optional.

The model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). It does not cover IGMP/MLD proxy or snooping, which are left to separate documents. No protocol-specific notifications are defined, but users can apply the subscription mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641 to its data nodes.
sections.eli5: IGMP and MLD are how computers ask to join a group broadcast. This RFC is the common settings sheet for the routers that listen to those requests.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The main goal is that the basic capabilities in the model are supported by any major existing implementation, and that other implementations can be expressed with optional features plus simple vendor augmentations. Occasionally implemented parameters become optional features. Rarely implemented ones are left out for augmentation. Operational state is mostly not tied to features, because a missing value can often be derived or defaulted harmlessly.

Some parameters were considered and deliberately left out, such as explicit tracking and last member query count at the global level, and passive mode, promiscuous mode and query before immediate leave at the interface level.

IGMP supports only IPv4 and MLD only IPv6, so they are separate schema branches. This lets a device support either or both independently, matches the style of RFC 8344, and accommodates their differences more cleanly.
sections.eli5: The model includes the settings almost every router has, and offers the rarer ones as optional extras, like add-on buttons.

sections.title: Module Structure
sections.content:
The model augments the core routing model of RFC 8349. The igmp and mld containers sit under control-plane-protocol in /rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols. The igmp container instantiates IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or IGMPv3, and the mld container instantiates MLDv1 or MLDv2. Several instances are possible, though an implementation MAY restrict that. Operational state sits beside its configuration in the same hierarchy.

Each subtree has three levels:

  • Global: settings and state for the whole protocol instance on the router.
  • Interface-global: defaults for every interface that does not set its own value.
  • Interface: settings and state for one interface. A value here overrides the interface-global value of the same name.

Global state includes entry and group counts and statistics for errors, messages received and messages sent. Per-interface settings include query-interval, query-max-response-time, last-member-query-interval, robustness-variable, version and, as features, immediate-leave, static-group and ssm-map. Read-only state includes the interface querier and the groups and sources learned.
sections.eli5: There are three control panels: one for the whole router, one with default settings for all its ports, and one for each port. A port's own setting wins over the default.

sections.title: The clear-groups Action
sections.content: IGMP and MLD each have one action, clear-groups, that clears group membership cache entries for that protocol. The input chooses either one interface by name or all interfaces, and gives a group address and a source address. The action is itself an optional feature (action-clear-groups).
sections.eli5: It is a reset button that wipes the router's list of who wants which broadcast, either on one port or on all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with other YANG modules, access is via NETCONF or RESTCONF, with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports. NACM (RFC 8341) can limit which users reach which operations and content.

Writable nodes under the igmp and mld subtrees are sensitive. Changing the global, interface-global or interface configuration can cause membership to be deleted or reconstructed on all interfaces or on a specific one. Unauthorized access could lead to network malfunctions and delivery of packets to inappropriate destinations. Read access can disclose operational state, and unauthorized use of clear-groups can delete membership records.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people should be allowed to change these settings or press the reset button, because mistakes can send broadcasts to the wrong places.
